title: Close up an engine air cleaner whose lid was clipped down over a filter element riding on its seat wall
justification: Changing the panel element in a clip-lid air cleaner is routine, regular work for automotive service technicians and mechanics (O*NET 49-3023: 'perform routine and scheduled maintenance services such as oil changes, lubrications, and tune-ups'; about 0.8 M in the US, figure to be confirmed) and for quick-lube technicians. The air-cleaner close-up is also a station on engine-dress lines. Closing the lid over an element whose urethane rim sits on the seat wall instead of in its groove is the classic error: unfiltered air bypasses the rim, wearing the cylinders and fouling the MAF sensor. The recovery forces something a clean close-up does not. The half-thrown clip is loaded by the cocked lid and has to be released under control. Then, once the element is down in its groove, the lid has to be held down against the element's seal by one hand while the other swings each spring clip over its catch and past centre. The clips are 18 cm apart and the lid springs off the catch as soon as it is let go, so one hand can't do both.
fault: The element's front rim (the side facing the robot) sits on top of the base's seat wall, 9 mm high and tilted about 2.5 deg; its rear rim is in the groove. The lid is on its two rear tabs and rests on the element, its front edge standing about 9 mm proud. The right front clip is hooked over the lid's catch but its lever stands half-thrown, short of centre and loaded by the lid; the left clip hangs open. The starting state is at rest after the settle. The front gap, the cocked lid and the half-thrown lever are visible from the cameras.
instruction: Close up the air cleaner properly, with the filter in it.
objects: Filter element: SimReady consumable_air_filter_engine_a01 (191 x 204 x 50 mm panel filter, mass set to 0.25 kg; rim treated as rigid). Air-cleaner housing fixed on a bench stand, centre x 0.30, y 0. It is built in mechkit from one real OEM housing's measurements (to be chosen, e.g. a common Toyota or Honda panel-filter box) and its photo or drawing. Lower box: PP-T20, about 262 x 246 x 120 mm, with seat groove, two rear tab slots and two front clip pivots 180 mm apart on the robot-facing side. The SimReady airSystem_air_filter_box_a01 is a single welded body (307 x 204 x 295 mm), usable only as a visual reference. Lid: about 0.35 kg on a gravity hinge at its rear tabs (opening limit about 100 deg). Seal compression is a sprung lid joint: about 2 mm travel at the front edge, with force measured from the real element (estimated 50 to 80 N). Two spring-steel clips: hinged levers with a hook. Over-centre is modelled with a spring target that flips past the dead point, and the lid is locked while both clips are past centre and hooked. Throw force is measured (estimated 15 to 30 N). Distractors (loose, at least 6 cm off the paths): folded shop towel (consumable_microfiber_towel_folded_large_a01), glove box (box_glove_a01), portable work light (lighting_taskLight_portableWork_a01).
skill: Release a half-thrown, loaded over-centre clip without letting the lid slap. Swing the lid up on its rear tabs, either holding it or taking it past 95 deg where it stays. Drop the element's rim into its groove all round. Lower the lid. Then one gripper holds it down against the seal near a clip (about 30 to 40 N) while the other swings that clip up, hooks the catch and pushes the lever past centre; repeat at the second clip. This is two-armed by force and geometry. Run limit 2,400 steps.
scoring: Scored only after both grippers have been at least 3 cm from housing, lid, clips and element for 2 s. Real trial: hands off, then feelers, then open the lid to inspect. Element seated: all four rim corners within 1.5 mm of the groove floor and tilt under 1.5 deg (real: no part of the rim on the wall, by eye once the lid is open). Lid closed: front-edge gap at most 1.0 mm at both clips (a 1.0 mm feeler won't enter). Clip locked: lever past its over-centre point with the hook on the catch. 1.0: element seated, lid closed, both clips locked. 0.5: element seated, lid closed, one clip locked. 0.25: element seated, lid not closed or no clip locked. 0: element not seated, including any state with the rim still on the wall even if both clips are closed, or element outside the housing at the end. No whole-run latch is needed: forcing the lid shut over the raised rim is blocked by contact in the simulation, and in the real trial it is caught by the inspection after opening.
nearest: #1973 close-a-swing-top-bottle (accepted): an over-centre wire bail pulled onto a rubber seal, one closure, no part to reseat. #42 Release a two-latch lid and lift it out with both hands (accepted): release only. #1957 Replace the cabin air filter behind a car's glove box (pending): a slide-in filter, no clips. #1136 Close a picture frame back and turn its four clips (accepted). #2264 Close a telescoping-lid box over its product without wedging the lid (revising). None starts from a lid half-latched over a mis-seated seal, or needs the lid held compressed while clipping.
risks: Lens fit: this is mostly a service job; on engine lines the air cleaner usually arrives assembled, so the factory claim is secondary. Reviewers may class 'press a lid and close two over-centre clips' as covered by #1973 and #42. The element reseat on its own is easy, so the difficulty must come from the held compression and the clip throws, with real forces. Clip positions, catches, seal travel and force, and clip throw force must come from one real housing (photo plus spring-scale measurements). Do not move clips toward the robot (#2383) and do not soften the seal for the demo (#1470). Modelling limits to state in fidelity: the lid is hinged on its tabs and cannot be lifted off; the element and its rim are rigid. Real hardware is affordable: an OEM housing and element cost about $60 to 120.
reviewer_reasons: Score is 10 x P(accept) about 0.2 x P(built in a day) about 0.35. This is the strongest of the six. Automotive service technicians and mechanics (49-3023) number well over 500k, and changing the engine air filter falls under their O*NET 'routine and scheduled maintenance'. #1555 failed only because small-engine mechanics are under 500k, so it doesn't count against this one. No clip-lid airbox task is on the board; the nearest are #1973 (swing-top bail), #42 (release only) and #1957 (cabin filter, pending, no clips). It uses a real, affordable OEM housing with a real mechanism: hinged lid, over-centre clips, seal groove. Weaknesses: (1) Our #2400 lesson. Once the half-thrown clip is released, what remains is the ordinary close-up: lift the lid, drop the element in, close, clip. That is judged on its own difficulty, and #2127 shows 'insufficient physical ability' gets final rejections. (2) The two-arm claim rests on 'the lid springs off unless held'. Over-centre airbox clips exist to draw the lid down onto the seal, so a reviewer comparing this with the real housing (#2383, #2379) may call the held compression invented, or forced by where the hook catches. (3) Clip positions, seal travel and force are still 'to be measured' from a housing that hasn't been chosen. Build: a lid hinge, a sprung front edge, two lever clips with over-centre spring targets and hook locks, and a loose rigid element that drops into a groove are all standard mechkit parts. The risks are opening the lid to 95 deg with a top-down gripper, swinging levers on the robot-facing wall, and getting the element to settle in the groove to within 1.5 mm.
reviewer_fix: Choose the OEM housing now and measure on it how far the clip hook reaches compared with the lid gap, and what forces the seal and the clip throw need. That shows whether a clip really can't hook or go past centre unless the lid is held down. If the real clips pull the lid down one-handed, the two-arm case and most of the difficulty go, so find out before building.
